$comment: California employment corpus. Almost every obligation here attaches at the first employee rather than at scale, and the ones that do have thresholds cluster at five. Dollar figures are expressed as formulas because California recalculates them each January; the reference values live in taxonomy.json under californiaReference.

clauses.title: Headcount Thresholds Now in Scope
clauses.rationale: California obligations switch on at headcount boundaries rather than phasing in, so crossing one turns on several duties at once — usually without any notice from the state.
clauses.body: The Company has {{headcountBand}}. At this size the following are in scope: {{headcountTriggers}}. These thresholds count all employees, including part-time, temporary, and seasonal, and in most cases they count employees anywhere rather than only those in California. Obligations attach the moment the threshold is crossed, not at the start of the next year, so re-run this check whenever headcount changes.

clauses.title: Wage Theft Prevention Act Notice
clauses.rationale: Required in writing at hire for every non-exempt employee, and again within seven days of any change not reflected on the wage statement. It is separate from the offer letter and is not satisfied by it.
clauses.body: At the time of hiring, give each employee a written [[wage theft notice]] in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information. It must state the rate or rates of pay and the basis, whether hourly, shift, day, week, salary, piece, commission or otherwise, including any overtime rates; allowances claimed as part of the minimum wage, including meal or lodging allowances; the regular payday; the employer's name including any "doing business as" names; the physical address of the main office or principal place of business, and a mailing address if different; the employer's telephone number; the name, address and telephone number of the workers' compensation carrier; a statement that the employee may accrue and use paid sick leave, has a right to request and use it, may not be terminated or retaliated against for using or requesting it, and may complain about retaliation; and the existence of any federal or state emergency or disaster declaration that applies to the county or counties of employment, was issued within thirty (30) days before the employee's first day, and may affect their health and safety during employment. The Labor Commissioner publishes a template. A temporary services employer must additionally give the name, physical and mailing address and telephone number of the legal entity for whom the employee will perform work. Notify the employee in writing of any change to this information within seven (7) calendar days, unless every change is reflected on a timely wage statement or is provided in another writing required by law within seven days. The notice is not owed to every worker: "employee" here excludes anyone directly employed by the state or a political subdivision, anyone exempt from overtime by statute or wage order, and anyone covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement providing premium overtime rates and a regular hourly rate at least thirty percent above the state minimum wage.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §2810.5 (as amended by Stats. 2023, Ch. 451 (AB 636), eff. Jan. 1, 2024)

Two items the earlier check listed as NOT confirmed — the main office address and the telephone number — are in §2810.5(a)(1)(E) and (F) and are confirmed, with the mailing address conditioned on being different from the physical one. Two requirements the clause did not have are now in it: the paid sick leave statement in (a)(1)(H), which the earlier check had not noticed at all, and the disaster declaration in (a)(1)(I) with its thirty-day and health-and-safety qualifiers. Full record in verification/findings/can_wtpa.json. NOT primary-verified: no human has read or signed this.
defects: No decision construing §2810.5 was found on CourtListener. The one hit was a passing reference in Turrieta v. Lyft. The section appears unconstrued, so every ambiguity in it is open.

§2810.5(a)(4) and (d) require an employer of an H-2A agricultural worker to give a separate Spanish-language section describing a long list of additional rights, using the Labor Commissioner's template, from 15 March 2024. It was read and is not carried, because the corpus is not aimed at agricultural employers. An agricultural employer following this clause would be short of the section.

§2810.5(a)(1)(J) lets the Labor Commissioner add any other information deemed material and necessary. The clause states the statutory list and notes the template; it cannot state what the Labor Commissioner has added, and this session did not open the Labor Commissioner's published template.
No penalty for failing to give the notice is stated in §2810.5 itself and none was researched. The clause states a duty with no consequence attached.

clauses.title: Pay Scale on Request
clauses.rationale: Applies to every California employer regardless of size, and separately requires the pay scale for a current employee's own position on request.
clauses.body: Provide the pay scale for a position to any applicant who has completed an initial interview and requests it, and to any current employee who requests the scale for their own position. Pay scale means the salary or hourly range the employer reasonably expects to pay, not a placeholder range wide enough to be meaningless.

clauses.title: Pay Scale in Job Postings
clauses.rationale: At fifteen employees the scale must appear in the posting itself. The obligation reaches third-party job boards the employer uses, which is where it is most often missed.
clauses.body: The Company has {{headcountBand}} and must include the pay scale in every job posting, including postings placed through a third party. Retain the job description and pay scale for each position for the duration of employment plus three (3) years; those records are open to inspection by the Labor Commissioner.

clauses.title: Salary History Ban
clauses.rationale: The prohibition covers agents and recruiters too, and volunteered history cannot be used to justify a pay disparity on its own.
clauses.body: Do not ask an applicant about salary history, and do not rely on it in deciding whether to make an offer or what to offer. This applies to anyone acting on the Company's behalf, including recruiters and background check vendors. If an applicant volunteers the information without prompting, it may be considered, but it cannot by itself justify a pay differential.

clauses.title: State Benefit Notices and Pamphlets
clauses.rationale: These are distributed at hire and again at the triggering event. Failure to distribute is cited routinely in agency audits because it is trivial to verify.
clauses.body: Distribute at hire: the State Disability Insurance and Paid Family Leave pamphlets, the workers' compensation rights notice and carrier information, the Civil Rights Department sexual harassment pamphlet, the paid sick leave notice, and the Company's written policies. Redistribute the disability and paid family leave notices when an employee takes a qualifying leave.

clauses.title: New Hire Reporting
clauses.rationale: Twenty days from start of work, per employee, with a per-employee penalty. Payroll providers usually handle it, but the obligation stays with the employer.
clauses.body: Report each new or rehired employee to the Employment Development Department on Form DE 34 within twenty (20) days of their first day of work. Confirm whether the payroll provider files this; the duty remains the Company's whether or not it does.

clauses.title: Mandatory Workplace Postings
clauses.rationale: Remote and distributed workforces do not remove the obligation; the notices have to reach employees by the means normally used for workplace communication.
clauses.body: Post in a conspicuous place accessible to all employees: the wage order for the Company's industry, payday notice, minimum wage notice, safety and health protection, workers' compensation rights, unemployment and disability insurance, paid sick leave, discrimination and harassment rights, whistleblower rights, family and medical leave rights, emergency contact information, and any local ordinance notice. Where employees work remotely, distribute the same notices electronically by the means normally used for workplace communications.

clauses.title: Local Ordinance Check
clauses.rationale: Dozens of California cities and counties set their own minimum wage and paid leave rules above the state floor, and the applicable one is set by where the employee works, not where the company sits.
clauses.body: Check the minimum wage, paid sick leave, and fair scheduling ordinances of every city and county where an employee physically works, including a remote employee's home city. Local rates commonly exceed the state minimum and carry their own posting and notice requirements. Where state and local rules differ, the one more favorable to the employee applies.

clauses.title: Injury and Illness Prevention Program
clauses.rationale: Required of every California employer with any employee, including office-only and fully remote workplaces. It is the first document Cal/OSHA requests in any inspection, and not having one is a standalone citation.
clauses.body: Establish and maintain a written [[IIPP|iipp]] identifying the person responsible, the system for ensuring compliance, how hazards are communicated to employees, the procedure for investigating injuries, how hazards are corrected, and the training program. Keep records of training and of hazard inspections. The program applies to office and remote workplaces, not only to industrial ones.

clauses.title: Workplace Violence Prevention Plan
clauses.rationale: A separate written plan from the safety program, with its own training and its own log. The narrow exemption for very small worksites closed by the time the Company reaches this headcount.
clauses.body: Maintain a written [[Workplace Violence Prevention Plan|workplace violence prevention plan]] covering employee involvement, hazard identification, incident response, post-incident procedures, and training. Train employees at rollout and annually. Maintain a violent incident log recording each incident, and retain the log, training records, and hazard assessments for five (5) years. This plan is separate from the IIPP required by <<xr:can_iipp>>.

clauses.title: Harassment Prevention Training
clauses.rationale: Five employees is the trigger, and temporary and seasonal workers count toward it. Supervisors need double the hours and a shorter deadline after promotion.
clauses.body: An employer regularly employing five or more persons — counting people who provide services under a contract, not only payroll employees — must provide at least two (2) hours of classroom or other effective interactive training on sexual harassment to every supervisory employee and at least one (1) hour to every non-supervisory employee in California, and must repeat it for each employee once every two (2) years. A new non-supervisory employee is trained within six (6) months of hire; a new supervisory employee within six (6) months of assuming the supervisory position. A seasonal or temporary employee, or any employee hired to work for less than six months, is trained within thirty (30) calendar days after hire or within one hundred (100) hours worked, whichever comes first; for a temporary employee placed by a temporary services employer, the staffing agency trains them, not the client. The training must include information and practical guidance on the federal and state law prohibiting, preventing and correcting sexual harassment and on the remedies available to victims, practical examples aimed at instructing supervisors in preventing harassment, discrimination and retaliation, prevention of abusive conduct as a component, and harassment based on gender identity, gender expression and sexual orientation with its own practical examples; and it must be presented by trainers with knowledge and expertise in those areas. An employer may build its own module or direct employees to the Civil Rights Department's own online courses, which are deemed to satisfy the obligation. Understand what compliance buys and does not buy: a claim that the training did not reach a particular individual does not by itself make the employer liable, and complying does not insulate the employer from liability for harassment. The remedy for a violation is that the Department may seek an order requiring the employer to comply. NOT VERIFIED: this clause previously required records of completion to be retained for a minimum of two years. That requirement is not in Government Code section 12950.1; it comes from the Civil Rights Department's regulations, and the publisher of the California Code of Regulations, govt.westlaw.com, returns HTTP 403 at this environment's egress proxy, so no version of it was read. Retain records, and have a reviewer confirm the period and the form.

§12950.1(l) allows an employer in the construction industry with a multiemployer collective bargaining agreement to satisfy the requirement by verifying training received within the past two years elsewhere. §12950 — the separate obligation to distribute an information sheet or poster on sexual harassment — was not read and is not addressed. It is a different section with a different duty and a reader may assume this clause covers it.

clauses.title: Written Harassment and Discrimination Policy
clauses.rationale: The regulation prescribes what the policy must contain and requires distribution with a tracked acknowledgment. A generic handbook paragraph does not satisfy it.
clauses.body: Maintain a written policy that lists all protected categories, states that the prohibition covers coworkers and third parties, provides a complaint mechanism that does not require reporting to a direct supervisor, commits to a timely and impartial investigation with reasonable conclusions, prohibits retaliation, and identifies remedies. Distribute it and obtain a tracked acknowledgment. Translate it where ten percent (10%) or more of the workforce speaks another language.
defects: The regulation applies to employers with five or more employees. The clause states the duty unconditionally, so a smaller employer reads a binding obligation it does not have and gets no signal when it crosses the threshold.

The prescribed contents also include instructions to supervisors on reporting complaints, and identification of the Civil Rights Department and the federal EEOC as additional avenues for an employee. The clause lists six required elements and omits both, so a policy built from the clause is short of the regulation while appearing complete.
clauses.verificationNote: Checked by web search only against 3 independent sources; no source document was opened. Defect types: omitted-qualifier, omitted-requirement.

clauses.title: Fair Chance Act Procedure
clauses.rationale: The violation is usually procedural rather than substantive — asking too early, or rejecting without the written assessment and the waiting period.
clauses.body: This procedure applies to an employer with five (5) or more employees. Do not ask about conviction history, on an application or otherwise, and do not inquire into or consider it, until after a conditional offer of employment. Never consider, distribute, or disseminate an arrest not followed by conviction, a referral to or participation in a diversion program, or a conviction that has been sealed, dismissed, expunged, statutorily eradicated, pardoned, or covered by a certificate of rehabilitation. To deny the position solely or in part because of conviction history, first make an [[individualized assessment]] of whether that history has a direct and adverse relationship with the specific duties of the job that justify denying the position, considering the nature and gravity of the offense or conduct, the time that has passed since the offense or conduct and completion of the sentence, and the nature of the job held or sought; the results may be committed to writing but the statute does not require it. Then notify the preliminary decision in writing, stating the disqualifying conviction or convictions, enclosing a copy of the conviction history report if there is one, and explaining the right to respond and the deadline for doing so. The applicant has at least five (5) business days to respond, and five (5) additional business days if, within that first period, the applicant notifies the Company in writing that they dispute the accuracy of the report and are taking specific steps to obtain evidence supporting that. Consider what the applicant submits before making a final decision. Notify a final denial in writing, stating the denial, any existing procedure the Company has for the applicant to challenge it or request reconsideration, and the right to file a complaint with the Civil Rights Department — there is no statutory right of appeal. The section does not apply to a position for which a state or local agency is required by law to run a conviction history check, to a criminal justice agency, to a Farm Labor Contractor position, or where any state, federal, or local law requires a criminal background check or restricts employment based on criminal history. This is the [[Fair Chance Act|fair chance act]] procedure. NOT VERIFIED: the Civil Rights Department's regulations are understood to bar advertisements stating that people with criminal histories will not be considered, and to fix when the response period starts running where receipt cannot be confirmed. Neither rule appears in §12952 and the official publisher of the regulations was unreachable, so both are recorded here unconfirmed rather than stated as law.

clauses.title: Lactation Accommodation Policy
clauses.rationale: A written policy is required and must be distributed at hire and when an employee asks about parental leave. Denial of a break carries the same one-hour premium as a missed rest period.
clauses.body: Develop and implement a written lactation accommodation policy that states the employee's right to request accommodation, the process for making the request, the employer's obligation to respond, and the right to file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner for any violation. Include it in the employee handbook or set of policies made available to employees, distribute it to new employees on hiring and whenever an employee inquires about or requests parental leave, and give a written response to the employee whenever break time or a compliant location cannot be provided. Provide a reasonable amount of break time each time the employee needs to express milk; it runs concurrently with existing break time where possible, and break time that does not run concurrently with the rest time authorized by the applicable Industrial Welfare Commission wage order is unpaid. Break time is not required where providing it would seriously disrupt the operations of the employer. Provide a room or location — which may be the employee's normal workspace if it qualifies — that is not a bathroom, is in close proximity to the work area, is shielded from view and free from intrusion, is safe, clean and free of hazardous materials, and contains a surface for the pump and personal items, a place to sit, and access to electricity or an alternative such as an extension cord or charging station; and provide access to a sink with running water and a refrigerator, or another suitable cooling device, in close proximity to the workspace. A multipurpose room may be used, with lactation taking precedence over other uses while it is in use for that purpose, and a temporary location is permitted where operational, financial or space limitations require it, on the same conditions. An employer with fewer than fifty (50) employees may be exempt from a requirement on demonstrating that it would impose an undue hardship — significant difficulty or expense measured against the size, financial resources, nature or structure of the business — and where it is the room requirement that causes the hardship, must still make reasonable efforts to provide a location other than a toilet stall, in close proximity to the work area. Denial of reasonable break time or of adequate space is a failure to comply for purposes of Labor Code section 226.7, which carries one additional hour of pay, and the Labor Commissioner may separately cite the employer and impose a civil penalty of one hundred dollars ($100) for each day an employee is denied it. Do not discharge, discriminate or retaliate against an employee for exercising or attempting to exercise these rights.

clauses.title: Off-Duty Cannabis Use
clauses.rationale: Standard urine and hair tests detect non-psychoactive metabolites, which is precisely what the statute now bars employers from acting on. Testing programs written before this change are non-compliant by default.
clauses.body: Do not discriminate against an employee or applicant for cannabis use away from work and off Company premises, or on the basis of a test detecting non-psychoactive cannabis metabolites. Impairment at work may still be addressed, and testing that identifies active psychoactive compounds remains permitted. Review any existing drug testing program against this rule; construction and federally regulated safety-sensitive roles are treated differently.

clauses.title: Heat Illness Prevention
clauses.rationale: A written plan, water, shade, cool-down rests, and training are all separately citable, and the high-heat procedures attach at a lower temperature than most employers assume.
clauses.body: Maintain a written heat illness prevention plan covering provision of water, access to shade, cool-down rest periods, acclimatization for new and returning workers, emergency response, and training. High-heat procedures with additional observation and reminder requirements apply above the regulatory threshold. Indoor workplaces are covered by a parallel standard where indoor temperatures reach the applicable trigger.
defects: The clause asserts the indoor obligation but cites only 8 C.C.R. §3395, which governs OUTDOOR places of employment. The indoor duty lives in §3396. This is the same shape as the confirmed defect in ipa_state_carveout: a duty asserted under the number of a neighbouring section, so a reader who follows the citation to check the indoor rule will not find it there.

Section 3395 applies to outdoor places of employment. The clause opens with an unconditional "maintain a written heat illness prevention plan", giving an indoor-only employer no way to tell which standard applies to it.

The triggers are stated as "the regulatory threshold" and "the applicable trigger" rather than as numbers. That is defensible drafting for figures that move, but it means the clause cannot be checked against the source without going to the source.
clauses.verificationNote: Checked by web search only against 3 independent sources; no source document was opened. Defect types: miscitation, omitted-qualifier.

clauses.title: Privacy Notice for Employee Data
clauses.rationale: The HR data exemption expired. Applicants, employees, and contractors are now consumers, with notice, deletion, correction, and limitation rights over their own employment data.
clauses.body: Provide a notice at collection to applicants, employees, and contractors describing the categories of [[personal data]] collected, the purposes, retention periods, and any sale or sharing, and honor requests to know, delete, correct, and limit use of sensitive information. Applies where the Company meets the statutory revenue or volume thresholds. Monitoring of employees, including device and location tracking, must appear in this notice.

clauses.title: EDD Employer Registration
clauses.rationale: The registration trigger is a dollar threshold in a quarter, not the first hire, and the fifteen-day clock runs from crossing it.
clauses.body: An employing unit becomes an "employer" once it has, in the current or the preceding calendar year, one or more employees and pays wages for employment in excess of one hundred dollars ($100) in any calendar quarter; it must register with the Employment Development Department within fifteen (15) days of becoming one. Thereafter file a report of contributions, a quarterly return and a report of wages, and deposit withholding on the assigned schedule. Filing is not optional as to channel: since 1 January 2018 all employers must file the report of contributions, quarterly return and report of wages electronically, and an employer may only be excused on an approved waiver granted for lack of automation, severe economic hardship, a current federal electronic-filing exemption or other good cause, valid for a year or longer at the Director's discretion. Report every new employee who works in this state and to whom the employer anticipates paying wages, and every returning employee separated from the employer for at least sixty (60) consecutive days, within twenty (20) days of hiring; an employer transmitting electronically instead submits two monthly transmissions not less than twelve and not more than sixteen days apart. Personal liability is not automatic and does not attach to everyone: an officer, major stockholder, or other person having charge of the affairs of a corporate, association, limited liability partnership or limited liability company employing unit who WILFULLY fails to pay contributions or withholdings on the date they become delinquent is personally liable for the contributions, withholdings, penalties and interest, and the Director may assess that person directly.

clauses.title: Workers' Compensation Insurance
clauses.rationale: Required from the first employee with no small-employer exemption, and operating without it is a criminal offense that also strips the exclusive-remedy defense.
clauses.body: Obtain workers' compensation coverage before the first employee's first day. There is no small-employer exemption. Operating without coverage is a misdemeanor, carries a stop order and per-employee penalties, and allows an injured employee to sue in civil court rather than being limited to the compensation system. Post the carrier notice and provide the claim form within one working day of learning of an injury.

clauses.title: CalSavers Retirement Mandate
clauses.rationale: Registration is mandatory even for employers that have no intention of offering a plan — the only alternative is certifying an exemption, which itself requires action.
clauses.body: Either offer a qualifying employer-sponsored retirement plan or register for [[CalSavers|calsavers]] and facilitate employee payroll deductions. Employers with a qualifying plan must still certify their exemption. Doing nothing is not an option and carries a per-eligible-employee penalty that escalates if it remains uncured.

clauses.title: Cal-COBRA Continuation Coverage
clauses.rationale: Employers below the federal COBRA threshold often assume no continuation obligation exists. California fills that gap, and the notice duty sits with the carrier and the employer jointly.
clauses.body: Employers with two to nineteen employees fall under [[Cal-COBRA|cal-cobra]] rather than federal COBRA. Confirm the carrier issues the required election notices and that the Company notifies the carrier of a qualifying event within the statutory window. Once the Company reaches twenty employees, federal COBRA applies instead and the notice obligations shift.

clauses.title: Annual Pay Data Reporting
clauses.rationale: A separate report is required for labor contractor workers, and that second report is the one most commonly missed in the first filing year.
clauses.body: File an annual [[pay data report|pay data report]] with the Civil Rights Department covering the prior calendar year, reporting employee counts and pay bands by race, ethnicity, and sex within each job category, together with median and mean hourly rates. A separate report covers workers supplied by labor contractors. The Company has {{headcountBand}} and is within scope.

clauses.title: California Exempt Classification
clauses.rationale: California's salary floor is higher than the federal one and moves every January, and its duties test requires that more than half the employee's time is actually spent on exempt work — a quantitative test, unlike the federal standard.
clauses.body: To be exempt in California the {{workerLabel}} must clear an [[exempt salary threshold]] of at least {{caExemptSalary}} and must spend more than one half of their working time on exempt duties. The salary floor rises with {{caMinWage}}, so review this classification each January. Because California applies a quantitative duties test rather than a primary-duty test, a role that is exempt federally may still be non-exempt here.

clauses.title: Written Commission Agreement
clauses.benchmark: Required by statute wherever commissions are paid; frequently absent in early-stage sales hires
clauses.rationale: California requires a signed written commission plan with a receipt. Without one, disputes over when a commission is earned are resolved against the employer.
clauses.body: Where any part of compensation is commission, provide a signed written agreement setting out the method of computation and payment, and obtain a signed receipt. State expressly when a commission is earned, whether it survives termination, and how chargebacks operate. A commission that has been earned is wages and must be paid at separation under <<xr:ea_termination>>, regardless of any active-employment condition.

clauses.title: California Forum and Choice of Law
clauses.rationale: A Delaware corporation instinctively names Delaware law. For a California employee that provision is voidable at the employee's election, and the fee-shifting runs one way.
clauses.body: This agreement is governed by California law and any dispute is adjudicated in California. [[Labor Code §925|labor code 925]] applies to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017 with an employee who primarily resides and works in California. For such a contract the Company may not require, as a condition of employment, a provision that would make the {{workerLabel}} adjudicate a claim arising in California outside California, or that would deprive the {{workerLabel}} of the substantive protection of California law in a controversy arising in California; adjudication includes both litigation and arbitration. Such a provision is voidable by the {{workerLabel}}, and if it is voided at their request the matter is adjudicated in California and California law governs. In addition to [[injunctive relief]] and any other remedies available, a court may award reasonable attorney's fees to an employee enforcing the section. Section 925 does not apply to a contract with an employee who is in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the venue, forum, or choice-of-law term.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §925
CourtListener — LGCY Power, LLC v. Superior Court (Cal. Ct. App., 5th Dist., Mar. 1, 2022)

defects: The clause states §925 and stops. It does not tell the reader what happens if the employee never invokes it — the provision is voidable, not void, so an unexercised right leaves the contrary forum clause standing.

No published decision construing "primarily resides and works" was found. For a remote employee who resides outside California but works into it, or the reverse, the clause states the test without resolving it.

clauses.title: Arbitration Limits in California
clauses.benchmark: Present in 38% of California employment agreements; among the most litigated provisions in the state
clauses.rationale: California unconscionability doctrine sets specific structural requirements, federal law carves out sexual harassment and assault claims, and an employer that misses an arbitration fee deadline waives the right outright.
clauses.body: If the Company uses arbitration, the agreement must be a separate signed document, mutual, and must provide a neutral arbitrator, adequate discovery, a written award subject to review, all remedies otherwise available, and payment by the Company of all costs unique to arbitration. It cannot compel sexual harassment or assault claims. Missing an arbitration fee deadline is a material breach that waives the right to arbitrate and returns the case to court.

clauses.title: Release and Section 1542 Waiver
clauses.benchmark: Present in 96% of California separation agreements
clauses.rationale: A general release that does not expressly waive Section 1542 does not reach unknown claims, which is the main thing the release was bought for.
clauses.body: A general release does not extend to claims the releasing party does not know or suspect to exist in their favour at the time of execution and that, if known, would have materially affected the settlement. A release meant to reach unknown claims should waive [[Civil Code §1542|section 1542]] expressly and quote it as it currently reads, amended effective 1 January 2019; but the words are not what decides it. The section exists to stop a mere recital from barring a later-discovered claim in the absence of conscious understanding, so what matters is whether this employee actually understood what was being given up and whether they were advised. Four things a release cannot do. It cannot release wages already due unless those wages have been paid — a release taken in breach of that rule is null and void and taking it is a misdemeanour. It cannot compromise a workers' compensation claim without the approval of the appeals board or a referee. It cannot waive unemployment benefits, which are not subject to assignment, release or commutation. And in an agreement related to separation from employment it cannot prohibit disclosure of information about unlawful acts in the workplace — meaning harassment, discrimination or other conduct the employee has reasonable cause to believe is unlawful — and any non-disparagement or workplace-conditions restriction must carry, in substantial form, the words "Nothing in this agreement prevents you from discussing or disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace, such as harassment or discrimination or any other conduct that you have reason to believe is unlawful." A general release of all claims is still permitted in a separation agreement provided it is otherwise lawful, the amount paid may still be kept confidential, and trade secrets and confidential information not involving unlawful acts may still be protected. Before the employee signs, tell them in the agreement that they have the right to consult an attorney and give them at least five (5) business days to do so; they may sign sooner only if that choice is knowing and voluntary and was not induced by pressure or by different terms for signing early.

California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §206.5 (release of wages due)

defects: The previous body said a release cannot waive "the right to file with or participate in an agency investigation". Gov. Code §12964.5(a)(1)(A)(ii) forbids requiring that release in exchange for a raise or bonus or as a condition of employment or continued employment. It is not a blanket rule about separation agreements: §12964.5(b)(3) permits a general release of all claims in a separation agreement, and §12964.5(d)(1) takes negotiated settlements of filed claims outside the section entirely. The rebuilt clause states the separation-agreement rules and does not repeat the blanket claim, but it also does not resolve what an employer may ask for at the point of hire, which is where the prohibition actually bites.

Federal law was not read. An age-discrimination waiver in a separation agreement is governed by the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act, whose consideration and revocation periods are longer than the five business days §12964.5(b)(4) requires. An employer following this clause for an employee over forty would be short.
Code of Civil Procedure §1001, which restricts confidentiality in settlements of certain harassment and discrimination claims, was not read. It overlaps §12964.5 and may impose more.

clauses.title: California Overtime
clauses.rationale: California computes overtime daily as well as weekly and adds double time. An employer paying on the federal weekly rule alone underpays every long day.
clauses.body: Non-exempt employees receive time and one half for hours over eight (8) in a workday and over forty (40) in a workweek, and for the first eight hours on the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek. Double time applies over twelve (12) hours in a day and beyond eight hours on the seventh consecutive day. The regular rate used for overtime includes non-discretionary bonuses and shift differentials, not base pay alone.

clauses.title: Reporting Time and Split Shift Pay
clauses.rationale: Both premiums are routinely missed because payroll systems do not compute them, and they surface in aggregate in wage claims.
clauses.body: An employee who reports for a scheduled shift and is given less than half the scheduled hours is owed [[reporting time pay]] of half the scheduled shift, a minimum of two (2) and a maximum of four (4) hours at the regular rate. An employee whose workday is interrupted by an unpaid, non-meal break is owed a [[split shift]] premium of one hour at the minimum wage. Both are owed in addition to hours actually worked.

clauses.title: California Paid Sick Leave
clauses.rationale: Local ordinances frequently exceed the state floor, and combining sick leave into a single unlimited PTO bucket forfeits the ability to apply the statutory caps.
clauses.body: Employees accrue paid sick leave at {{caSickAccrual}}, with a minimum entitlement of {{caSickMinimum}}. Accrued balance must appear on the wage statement or a separate written notice each pay period. Sick leave may be used for the employee or a family member, and for a designated person. The Company may not require a doctor's note for statutory sick leave, may not count its use against attendance, and may not require the employee to find a replacement. Local ordinances may require more; the more generous provision applies.

sources.title: Legal Aid at Work — SB 616 increases paid sick leave from 3 to 5 days
CDF Labor Law — New California paid sick leave requirements
LegiScan — CA SB616 text

clauses.verificationNote: Search summary supports: accrual of one hour per thirty hours worked from commencement of employment; minimum entitlement of forty hours or five days; accrual and carryover cap of eighty hours; annual use may be limited to forty hours or five days; local ordinances may require more. NOT confirmed by the search: use available from the ninetieth day of employment, and the requirement that the accrued balance appear on the wage statement or a separate written notice each pay period.

clauses.title: California Family Rights Act Leave
clauses.rationale: CFRA attaches at five employees, not fifty, and its definition of family is broader than the federal one — which means leave that is CFRA-protected but not FMLA-protected does not run concurrently.
clauses.body: Employees with at least twelve (12) months of service and one thousand two hundred fifty (1,250) hours in the prior year are entitled to twelve (12) weeks of job-protected [[CFRA|cfra]] leave in a twelve-month period. Covered family members include a child, parent, parent-in-law, grandparent, grandchild, sibling, spouse, domestic partner, and one designated person per year. The Company has {{headcountBand}}, which is above the five-employee threshold. Maintain group health coverage during leave and restore the employee to the same or a comparable position.

clauses.title: Pregnancy Disability Leave
clauses.rationale: PDL is separate from CFRA and stacks with it, so an employee can be entitled to four months plus twelve weeks. Treating them as one bucket is a common and expensive error.
clauses.body: [[Pregnancy disability leave]] provides up to four (4) months of job-protected leave for disability related to pregnancy, childbirth, or a related condition, with no minimum service requirement. It is separate from and additional to CFRA leave under <<xr:hb_ca_cfra>>, so an eligible employee may take both in sequence. Reasonable accommodation and transfer obligations apply independently of leave.

clauses.title: Bereavement and Reproductive Loss Leave
clauses.rationale: Two separate entitlements, each five days, each attaching at five employees, and both frequently absent from handbooks written before they existed.
clauses.body: Provide up to five (5) days of bereavement leave on the death of a family member, and up to five (5) days of reproductive loss leave following a failed adoption or surrogacy, miscarriage, stillbirth, or unsuccessful assisted reproduction. Days need not be consecutive. Leave may be unpaid where the Company has no paid policy, but employees may use accrued paid leave. Both entitlements require confidentiality as to the reason.

clauses.title: Coordinating CFRA and FMLA
clauses.rationale: The two laws overlap but do not match. Designating leave as running concurrently when only one law covers it shortens the employee's entitlement unlawfully.
clauses.body: The Company has {{headcountBand}}, so federal FMLA applies alongside CFRA under <<xr:hb_ca_cfra>>. The two run concurrently only where both cover the reason. Pregnancy disability is FMLA-covered but not CFRA-covered, so it runs against FMLA while CFRA baby-bonding leave remains available afterward. Leave for a parent-in-law, grandparent, sibling, or designated person is CFRA-only. Designate each leave against the correct statute in writing rather than assuming they overlap.

clauses.title: Personnel and Payroll Record Requests
clauses.rationale: Two different deadlines for two different record types, each with its own penalty, and a request often arrives as the opening move in a wage claim.
clauses.body: Respond to a request for personnel records within thirty (30) calendar days, and to a request for payroll records within twenty-one (21) calendar days. The obligation continues for one (1) year after separation. Missing either deadline carries a penalty and, in practice, signals to the requesting party that records were not maintained. Retain personnel records for at least four (4) years.

clauses.title: California ABC Test
clauses.rationale: Prong B is the one that defeats most engagements, and it is not curable by contract language. A software company engaging a software developer as a contractor fails it regardless of how the agreement is drafted.
clauses.body: California presumes a worker is an employee. To engage them as a contractor the Company must satisfy all three prongs of the [[ABC test|abc test]]: (A) the worker is free from the Company's control and direction in fact as well as under this agreement; (B) the work is outside the usual course of the Company's business; and (C) the worker is customarily engaged in an independently established trade of the same nature. Prong B cannot be satisfied by contract language. Because the Company's business is {{industryName}}, an engagement for work of that same nature is unlikely to qualify. Misclassification exposure includes unpaid wages, overtime, meal and rest premiums, business expenses, payroll taxes, and penalties, and can reach individuals personally.

sources.citation: Dynamex Operations W. v. Superior Court, 4 Cal.5th 903 (2018)

clauses.title: Statutory Exemptions from the ABC Test
clauses.rationale: The exemptions do not make someone a contractor — they only swap in the older multi-factor test, which the engagement still has to pass.
clauses.body: Certain occupations and relationships are exempt from the ABC test and are instead evaluated under the older multi-factor common law standard, including some professional services, licensed practitioners, and genuine business-to-business contracting relationships. Each exemption carries its own conditions, commonly including a business licence, a separate business location, the ability to set rates, and contracting with other clients. Document which exemption is being relied on and which of its conditions are met; an exemption is not a conclusion that the worker is a contractor.

clauses.title: Freelance Worker Protection Act
clauses.rationale: Applies to most small freelance engagements, requires a written contract and record retention, and prohibits conditioning payment on accepting less than the agreed amount.
clauses.body: The Freelance Worker Protection Act applies only to contracts entered into or renewed on or after 1 January 2025, and only to "professional services" as the Labor Code defines that term — a closed list that includes marketing, human resources administration, graphic design, grant writing, fine art, freelance writing, translating, editing, illustration and photography, and a number of licensed trades, and does not include work outside it. A freelance worker is a person, or an organisation of no more than one person, retained as a bona fide independent contractor for an amount of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) or more, counting either that contract alone or all contracts between the same hiring party and contractor in the immediately preceding one hundred twenty (120) days. Put the contract in writing, furnish the freelancer a signed copy physically or electronically, and retain it for no less than four (4) years. It must state the name and mailing address of each party; an itemised list of all services, including the value of those services and the rate and method of compensation; the date the hiring party will pay or the mechanism for determining it; and the date by which the freelancer must submit a list of services rendered to meet the hiring party's internal processing deadlines. Pay by the contract date, or within thirty (30) days of completion of the services if the contract does not specify. Once the freelancer has begun work, do not require, as a condition of timely payment, that they accept less than the agreed compensation or that they provide more goods or services or grant more intellectual property rights than agreed. Do not discriminate or take adverse action that penalises the freelancer, or would reasonably be likely to deter them, for opposing a prohibited practice, participating in enforcement proceedings, or asserting rights under the Act. Any waiver of the Act is void. A freelancer or a public prosecutor may sue; a prevailing plaintiff is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees and costs and injunctive relief, with damages of one thousand dollars ($1,000) where a written contract was requested before work began and refused, up to twice the amount unpaid where payment was late, and the value of the contract or of the work performed for any other violation. Note that the Act does not displace ordinary contract law: an oral contract remains enforceable and a refusal to put the deal in writing does not defeat the freelancer's claim.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§18100, 18101, 18102, 18103, 18104, 18105, 18106 and 18107 (Freelance Worker Protection Act, added by Stats. 2024, Ch. 870 (SB 988))
California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Lab. Code §2778(b)(2), the definition of "professional services" §18101(c) adopts

defects: The "professional services" list in Lab. Code §2778(b)(2) runs from (A) to (O) and several entries carry their own conditions — marketing must be original and creative work depending primarily on the individual's invention, imagination or talent; freelance writing and the licensed trades have multi-part tests. The clause names representative categories and says the list is closed. It does not reproduce the conditions, so a hiring party cannot tell from this clause whether a particular engagement is inside the list.
No decision construing §§18100–18107 was found on CourtListener. The Act took effect on 1 January 2025 and appears to be entirely unconstrued.

Whether a contract entered into before 1 January 2025 and amended (as opposed to renewed) after that date comes within the Act was not resolved. §18107 says 'entered into or renewed', which is narrower than the formula other California statutes use.

clauses.title: Expense Exposure on Reclassification
clauses.rationale: Expense reimbursement is one of the largest components of a reclassification award, because it accrues across the whole engagement and carries interest and fees.
clauses.body: If the engagement is later reclassified as employment, California requires reimbursement of all necessary business expenses the worker bore, including equipment, software, mileage, and the business portion of phone and internet, for the entire period, with interest and attorney's fees. This exposure accrues from day one and is not reduced by the Contractor having agreed to bear its own costs.

clauses.title: California Safety and Violence Prevention Programs
clauses.rationale: Included in the formation package so a company standing up its first California hire sees the two written programs it needs before day one. The hiring package carries the full California set.
clauses.body: Before the first California employee starts, adopt a written Injury and Illness Prevention Program covering hazard identification, correction, communication, and training, and — once the Company has ten (10) or more employees — a separate written Workplace Violence Prevention Plan with its own training and violent incident log. Both apply to office and remote workplaces. These are the two programs Cal/OSHA asks for first in any inspection.

clauses.title: California Employer Registration Checklist
clauses.rationale: Four separate registrations, each with its own trigger and clock, and each carrying penalties assessed per employee.
clauses.body: Before the first California employee's first day: obtain workers' compensation coverage, which has no small-employer exemption; register with the Employment Development Department within fifteen (15) days of paying more than one hundred dollars ($100) in quarterly wages; register for or certify exemption from CalSavers; and report each new hire on Form DE 34 within twenty (20) days. Provide the Wage Theft Prevention Act notice at hire to every non-exempt employee.
defects: Electronic filing through e-Services for Business is mandatory absent an approved waiver. Neither clause in this pair says so.
The clause carries no citation at all while asserting five separate legal duties. Every assertion here is unverifiable as filed, because there is nothing recorded to verify it against.
